title: Monasteries as hospitals
hookLine: monks kept books, schools, herb gardens and infirmaries

lines: A BASKET CARRIED ACROSS THE YARD.
cards: Mint. Small square beds of herbs in neat rows behind a stone wall. A monk in a dark habit kneels between them, cutting leaves into a basket.
He isn't cooking dinner. He carries the basket across the yard to a long room where sick men lie in beds, to make a warm drink for a feverish old brother and a poultice for a farmer's cut hand.

teach.b: In the middle ages, a monastery might be the place where the sick were cared for. The reason goes back to a rule.
Benedict's Rule for monks gives a whole chapter to the sick, and puts their care before everything else, because in serving them, the monks serve Christ.
Behind that is Jesus's scene in Matthew where visiting the sick is visiting him, the same scene that kept some at the bedside in the plague years.
And the letter of James asks, in the King James Bible: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him".
So monasteries set aside an infirmary, a room for the sick, with a brother in charge of it, and kept a garden of healing herbs nearby.

teach.h: AN HERB GARDEN BY THE INFIRMARY.
teach.b: An old plan for an ideal monastery, kept at the abbey of Saint Gall, puts a physician's herb garden right beside the infirmary.

teach.h: BOOKS, SCHOOLS, AND A LAMP BY THE BED.
teach.b: They kept books too, a slower kind of care. In the scriptorium, monks and nuns copied scripture, prayers, and old books of medicine and learning, page by page.

Some monasteries ran schools, where boys, and in convents girls, learned to read. None of this was the main point. For the monks, the point was prayer, the psalms sung through the hours of day and night.
But prayer that takes Matthew seriously spills out into rooms with beds, gardens with herbs and shelves with books.
You could call these communities keepers of the light: a lamp kept burning in the chapel, by a sick bed, and over a page.

how: Christian religious orders and churches still run hospitals, clinics and hospices around the world, and some monasteries still keep herb gardens and infirmaries for their own sick members.

send a novice and hope for the best.
games.why: Benedict's Rule says care of the sick comes before everything, because in serving them the monks serve Christ.

practice: Picture a small pot of herbs on a windowsill, basil, mint, rosemary, whatever you like, and imagine pinching off a leaf and smelling your fingers.

Now think of someone who's sick or worn out, someone you could bring a cup of mint tea, a bowl of soup, or just your company. If you pray, pray for them; if you don't, hold them in mind, with the smell of the herb.

wordCard.voice: Infirmary. The room for the sick that medieval monasteries kept, with a garden of healing herbs close by, following Benedict's Rule to care for the sick before everything else.

carryVoice: Your line: keepers of the light. Care can be as small as a cup of tea. Until next time.
